meta.title: Fun with Q1: Scouring the First Euclid Data for Astrophysical Anomalies with AnomalyMatch
meta.authorsHtml: Pablo Gómez<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Giuseppe Galardi<sup>1</sup>, David O’Ryan<sup>1</sup>

abstract: The Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) provides a first glimpse at the survey that will ultimately cover a third of the sky. We present a systematic search for astrophysical anomalies across the full Q1 footprint — approximately 30 million source cutouts generated on-the-fly from ∼19.4 TB of survey mosaics — using AnomalyMatch, a semi-supervised active learning framework, and the streaming cutout generator Cutana. Each complete pass sustains a generation rate of ∼200 images per second and completes the entire data volume in 48–72 hours on ESA Datalabs. Starting from 35 known anomalies, we perform three iterative training runs with active learning and identify 8,547 anomaly candidates, achieving a 60% anomaly ratio among the top-ranked predictions, of which 95% lack prior literature associations. We characterise the pipeline’s computational performance and demonstrate scalability to Euclid’s upcoming Data Release 1 (∼30× the sky area).

blocks.html: The Euclid space telescope [1] is producing an unprecedented volume of wide-field optical and near-infrared imaging that will ultimately cover roughly one-third of the sky. The Euclid Quick Data Release 1 [Q1; 2] represents the first public data release, containing high-quality imaging of the Euclid deep field areas - approximately 63 square degrees of the sky. Mining these data for astrophysical anomalies, i.e. rare and scientifically valuable objects is a task well suited to automated methods given the scale of the dataset.

AnomalyMatch [3] is a semi-supervised, label-efficient anomaly detection framework requiring as few as five to ten labelled examples, with active learning support. In a search of the Hubble Legacy Archive (HLA), it uncovered 1,176 anomalies across 19 morphological classes from ∼100 million cutouts, 65% previously unreported [4].

Following that HLA legacy search [4], we use the term anomaly throughout in the morphological sense: a source whose visual appearance departs markedly from the ordinary population of galaxies, stars, and artefacts. These include mergers with tidal features, gravitational lens and arcs, ring galaxies, or otherwise strongly disturbed morphologies. The term thus denotes visual rarity within predominantly known morphological classes.

Anomaly detection in astronomical surveys is an active area of research, with approaches ranging from isolation forests with active learning [Astronomaly; 5] to self-supervised methods for gravitational lens mining [6]. Early Euclid Q1 searches have already yielded candidate gravitational lenses [7, 8], and the Galaxy Zoo citizen science programme has produced the first Q1 morphology catalogue [9]. With the data volume expected from the full survey, efficient and scalable detection methods are paramount.

In this work, we present the first general-purpose anomaly search across the full Q1 data release using AnomalyMatch v1.3.0, which includes streaming cutout support via the open-source high-performance cutout generator Cutana [10]1 and native multichannel data handling. We focus on the computational aspects of running such a search at scale and report 8,547 anomaly candidates that require further expert classification.
Our main contributions are:
• A systematic anomaly search across the entire Q1 footprint (∼30 million cutouts, ∼19.4 TB of mosaics),
• A characterisation of the AnomalyMatch+Cutana streaming pipeline in terms of throughput and re-source utilisation (Figure 2);
• 8,547 anomaly candidates from three iterative runs, demonstrating scalability to Euclid DR1 (∼30× the

AnomalyMatch2 is an open-source, semi-supervised FixMatch algorithm [11] with an EfficientNet backbone [12] and an active learning loop [3]. It frames anomaly detection as a binary classification problem (anomaly vs. nominal) and leverages both a small labelled dataset and abundant unlabelled data to train a model using consistency regularisation and pseudo-labelling. The interactive user interface enables experts to validate and correct model predictions, progressively refining detection performance through iterative retraining. The resulting anomaly score of a source is the direct output of this binary classifier: the softmax probability that the final layer of the exponential-moving-average evaluation model assigns to the anomaly class, in [0, 1].

blocks.html: We use AnomalyMatch v1.3.0 [3], which introduces features critical for this work: streaming prediction support via Cutana [10] for on-the-fly cutout generation from catalogue positions and survey mosaics as well as improved normalisation consistency and performance. The Cutana integration and streaming of cutout creation to AnomalyMatch enables us to process the roughly 30 million Q1 sources without pre-generating and storing cutout images, significantly reducing storage requirements while enabling a search throughput of approximately 200 images per second.

We use Euclid Q1 visible instrument (VIS)-band data [2], generating single-channel greyscale cutouts at 180–200 px resolution (varied due to computational time constraints), normalised with an asinh stretch [13].

The initial labelled dataset was assembled from concurrent Q1 works. We started with 10 gravitational lenses from [14], 19 jellyfish galaxies from [15], and 6 outstanding mergers from [16] as positive (anomaly) examples, together with 300 nominal galaxy images as well as artefacts and otherwise unremarkable objects such as stars. As unlabelled data for the semi-supervised learning (SSL) training, we randomly sampled ≈25 000 images from the Euclid MERge (MER) source catalogues. The labelled set was iteratively expanded through active learning across three training runs (see Section 3.1).

All training and inference was performed on ESA Datalabs3 [17], using NVIDIA L4 and L40S GPUs. We leverage the streaming cutout generation capability of Cutana [10] to generate the roughly 30 million source cutouts from the MER catalogue positions on-the-fly during prediction. This streaming approach eliminates the need to pre-generate and store terabytes of cutout images. Figure 2 shows the resource profile for a representative singlecatalogue run (∼598 k sources) on an L40S: the pipeline sustains ∼200 images s−1, with cutout generation accounting for ∼70% of wall-clock time. Extrapolating this throughput, each complete Q1 pass takes 48–72 hours, with three passes performed for the iterative training described in Section 3.1.

We performed three model training runs with varying numbers of active learning cycles (two, six, and four, respectively) to investigate the effect of training duration on anomaly detection. By comparing score distributions and anomaly types surfaced by each model, we assess whether additional cycles improve recall or introduce overfitting to specific anomaly classes.

blocks.html: The first two runs each searched approximately 90% and 75% of the Q1 footprint, respectively, while the third and final run covered its entirety. The first training run used the initial labelled dataset described in Section 2.1. After the first run, we investigated top-ranked 1 000 predictions and extracted additional labels for further model training, identifying 22 clear anomalies and 476 nominal images. These were added to the labelled set for the second training run, which then, again inspecting the top 1 000 sources - served to add 10 additional anomalies and 265 nominal images. A final third run with the fully expanded training set searched the complete Q1 footprint and produced the final results presented here. The resulting anomaly ratios among the top-scored predictions (42–70 % per run) show the potential for high-precision discoveries.

Table 1 summarises the anomaly candidates identified across all three iterations, where we screened the top 5 000 highest-scoring sources per run. Anomalies were classified based on visual inspection of each sources’ morphology. The primary anomaly detected, and easiest to identify, were galaxy-galaxy mergers with clear tidal features. However, more subtle features were also used, such as gravitational lens and arcs, star forming clumps, distortion of the galaxy, or the existence of galactic rings. This screening was carried out by a single expert (one of the authors) and is intended to flag candidates for follow-up rather than to establish a final classification; ambiguous sources were retained as candidates. Consequently, no independent duplicate labelling was performed and no inter-rater agreement can be quoted here. A multi-expert review, in which several astronomers label the same sources independently so that agreement can be measured and disagreements adjudicated, is being set up for the dedicated catalogue publication; it is beyond the scope of the present proof-of-concept study, which focuses on the feasibility and computational behaviour of the search at Euclid scale. Cross-matching against SIMBAD [18], and ESASky [19] was used for identification (where possible) of anomalies. This literature search also provides a preliminary assessment of existing literature associations. A full exploration of the anomalies identified and a detailed astrophysical classification will follow in a dedicated publication.

Across all runs, 60.5% of screened sources were classified as anomaly candidates, with per-run ratios ranging from 42% to 70%; the high-scoring tail of every model is thus dominated by genuine anomalies, although the second run is markedly less pure than the other two (see Section 4). Of the 8 547 candidates, 8 086 (94.6%) have no existing literature associations.

blocks.html: datasets. The HLA search [4] processed ∼100 million pre-generated 150 × 150 px JPEG cutouts in 2.5 days, corresponding to ∼460 images s−1 for inference alone. Our Q1 pipeline achieves ∼200 images s−1 end-to-end on larger 180–200 px cutouts, but this includes on-the-fly cutout generation from ∼19.4 TB of raw survey mosaics via Cutana. As shown in Figure 2, cutout generation accounts for ∼70% of the wall-clock time; the inference-only throughput (∼660 images s−1) thus exceeds the HLA rate despite the larger image size, reflecting improvements in the v1.3.0 prediction pipeline. The streaming approach eliminates the need for intermediate storage at the cost of additional compute per iteration.

The three successive models score sources differently as the labelled set grows (Figure 3). Because the models are not calibrated against one another, the raw score distributions differ markedly: the second model (six training cycles) is considerably more conservative, assigning far fewer sources to intermediate score ranges than the first (two cycles) or third (four cycles) models. All three models nevertheless agree that the vast majority of sources are uninteresting, concentrating >99 % of scores near zero.

Where the models diverge is in the high-scoring tail. The relationship is notably asymmetric. Sources that score highly in the first or third model typically receive scores below 0.15 from the second model, indicating that the second model does not recognise these as anomalous. Conversely, sources that the second model scores highly do often receive high scores from the first and third models as well, as visible in the middle block of Figure 3. This asymmetry can be partly explained by the second model’s training history: with six active-learning cycles it may have overfit on the few anomalous training examples. Edge-on galaxies are a notable exception — the second model misclassifies them as anomalies, we hence labelled those as nominal for the third run and the third model then successfully suppressed them.

The cross-model comparison underscores the value of ensembling: each training cycle refines the decision boundary differently, yielding partly non-overlapping high-scoring sets. Combining anomaly lists across runs produces a richer catalogue than any single model; developing principled ensemble and calibration strategies is an important direction for future work.

In its present form the model is therefore best understood as a ranker rather than a calibrated detector. Scores order sources within a run but carry no absolute meaning, and a given score value does not correspond to the same anomaly likelihood across runs. All cross-run comparisons in this work are consequently made on ranks rather than on score values, and the screening depth is defined by a fixed number of top-ranked sources rather than by a score threshold. This is workable at Q1 scale but will become limiting at DR1 scale, where a fixed screening budget must be allocated across far more data. Future work will explore calibrating the classifier output — for instance against a held-out labelled sample — so that a score threshold carries a stable interpretation and model runs become directly comparable.

blocks.html: A further caveat concerns the selection function of the search itself. The labelled set is seeded with known lenses, jellyfish galaxies, and mergers, and grows by inspecting the model’s own top-ranked predictions. Both mechanisms bias the search towards the anomaly classes already represented in the labels. Subclasses that are severely underrepresented among the labelled anomalies — and genuine “unknown unknowns”, i.e. anomalous objects unlike anything in the labelled set — are therefore likely to be recovered only at reduced efficacy, or to be missed entirely. The resulting candidate list should thus be read as a highpurity sample of the anomaly types the model has been taught, not as a complete census of everything unusual in Q1. Seeding with a more morphologically diverse label set, and sampling beyond the top-ranked tail during active learning, are natural mitigations we intend to explore.

Looking ahead to DR1, which will cover approximately 30× the sky area of Q1, a linear extrapolation suggests additional scaling and performance measures are required. Based on the throughput measured in Figure 2 (∼200 images s−1), this would require roughly 7.5 weeks on a single GPU, or proportionally less with parallel execution across multiple GPUs. The v1.3.0 multichannel support also opens the possibility of leveraging Euclid’s Near Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) near-infrared bands alongside VIS, potentially improving anomaly discrimination at the cost of increased computational requirements. Given the richness of the Q1 findings with VIS-only data, a combined VIS+NISP search of DR1 represents a compelling science case.

The fraction of unreferenced anomaly candidates (94%) is expected to grow substantially in DR1, as the wider sky coverage will include many fields not yet deeply studied by other surveys. This positions AnomalyMatch as a discovery engine for flagging rare astrophysical objects in the Euclid era, with detailed classification to follow in dedicated studies.

We note that the Q1 data release has been less extensively searched than, for example, the HLA, and it is likely that some of our findings occur concurrently with independent studies of Q1 by other groups. In particular, several anomalies we report may also be identified in concurrent work by the Euclid Consortium, given the active investigation of Q1 data across multiple science working groups [7, 8]. The high fraction of candidates without literature associations should therefore be read with care: because Q1 was released only recently, work on many of these same sources is plausibly ongoing in parallel and simply not yet published. The fraction is consequently an upper limit on genuinely new discoveries and a statement about the current state of the literature, rather than a measure of the intrinsic novelty of the candidates. It is reported here as a coarse indicator of follow-up potential, and the dedicated catalogue publication will revisit it once the Q1 literature has matured.

We have presented a systematic anomaly search across the Euclid Q1 data release, processing ∼30 million VISband cutouts from ∼19.4 TB of mosaics and identifying 8,547 anomaly candidates across three iterative passes. The AnomalyMatch+Cutana streaming pipeline sustains ∼200 images per second on a single GPU, scales linearly with catalogue size, and confirms the feasibility of SSL-based anomaly detection at Euclid scale. Starting from minimal labelled data, the iterative active learning approach enables rapid deployment on new datasets without large pre-existing training sets.

Future work will extend to DR1 (∼30× larger) with multichannel VIS+NISP data. Q1 anomaly catalogues and detailed astrophysical classifications will be presented in forthcoming publications. AnomalyMatch is freely available as open-source software.

This research made use of many open-source Python packages and scientific computing packages. These include Astropy [20–22], Matplotlib [23], Pandas [24], PyTorch [25], NumPy [26], SciPy [27], scikit-learn [28], scikit-image [29], and Pillow [30].
